lines: A furnace's temperature sensor reports the exact same reading, hour after hour.
The controller watching it, the dashboard showing it, and the statistical process control chart tracking it all agree that everything here looks perfectly stable.
Not one of them has any reason yet to think otherwise.
A rule built to catch a sudden jump has nothing to catch here, because nothing ever jumps.
A rule built to catch an impossible value has nothing to catch either, because the number itself is completely plausible for this furnace.
The only thing actually wrong is that the reading has stopped moving at all, and only a check on how much a value varies over a window of time ever notices that.
On that same fleet of sensors, a different one briefly reports a value that's not just unusual, it's physically impossible for anything to actually be.
A third sensor throws a handful of isolated extreme spikes.
A detector built around the typical value nearby, deliberately excluding the spike itself from that calculation, catches each one without ever being thrown off by the very thing it's hunting for.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal answers it.

Imagine a rule flags that frozen furnace reading as bad, and the system has to decide what happens to it next: delete it completely, or set it aside in a separate holding table with a label explaining why.
Does that choice actually matter to whoever investigates this furnace later?
answer: It does matter, quite a lot.

A rule can always turn out to be wrong, and the exact point a rule calls bad might be the one real event that explains what actually happened — deleting it outright destroys the only record anyone would ever have of it.

lines: A firmware update on one sensor quietly re-scales everything it reports from that moment forward.
Every single reading after the update still looks completely plausible on its own, nothing about any individual point seems wrong.
But the overall typical level of the signal visibly shifts, and that shift is exactly what a check built to look for a change in level, rather than a single data point, is designed to catch.
After an outage, a gateway resends a whole chunk of readings it had buffered up.
A key built from the series, the device's own timestamp, and the gateway's sequence number collapses that exact resend straight back down to a single copy of each reading.
Comparing the device's timestamp against the gateway's own receiving timestamp is what separates a reading that's simply arriving late from one whose clock has actually gone wrong.
Nothing in this whole pipeline ever actually gets deleted.
Every single point a rule flags keeps its exact place in the original series, completely untouched, exactly as it was recorded.
That same point also gets a separate entry in a quarantine table, carrying which specific rule fired and how severe the system judged it to be.
Run every one of these checks across the whole fleet of sensors at once.
They catch nearly every single fault that was deliberately planted into the data, while raising only a small number of false alarms along the way.
And running every one of those checks on every single reading costs only a small fraction of the time that each individual reading actually represents.
Pull the whole picture together: a windowed variance check, a range check, a spike detector built to resist the spike itself, and a check built specifically for a shift in level.
Add a key that collapses a replayed batch, a quarantine table that never once deletes anything, and a measured cost that comfortably keeps pace with the plant.
Not one of those four detection rules could have stood in for any of the others — each one was built to ask a genuinely different question of the exact same data.
One more case worth reasoning through before moving on.
Go back to the hook's furnace, knowing only this one fact about it: its reading never moves at all.
Working from that fact alone, which of the three named rules actually ends up catching it: the spike rule, the range rule, or the windowed variance check?
answer: The windowed variance check is the one that actually fires.

The furnace's value is completely plausible and it never jumps, so neither the range rule nor the spike rule has anything at all to flag — only a rule built to watch how a value moves over time ever catches this one.
